words.definition: A false show put on to hide reality or to impress people.
words.example: Under the pretense of admiring the paintings, he was really casing the gallery.
words.mnemonic: Contains "pretend" — it's putting on a pretend face.

words.definition: A person who falsely claims special knowledge or skill to cheat others.
words.example: The so-called doctor turned out to be a charlatan peddling sugar pills as a cancer cure.
words.mnemonic: Say "char-LATIN" — he spouts fake Latin to sound like a real physician.

words.definition: A showy swindler who sells fake cures or empty promises to a crowd.
words.example: At the fair, a grinning mountebank hawked a tonic he swore could regrow hair overnight.
words.mnemonic: MOUNT-a-BANK — from Italian "monta in banco," one who mounts a bench to hawk phony remedies.

words.definition: The act of fooling people by pretending to be someone you are not.
words.example: His imposture as a decorated colonel collapsed when a real veteran questioned his medals.
words.mnemonic: Contains "impostor" — it's the performance an impostor puts on.

words.definition: Something presented as real that is actually fake or hollow.
words.example: The charity gala was a sham, funneling every donated dollar into the organizer's pocket.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "shame" — a fake thing that ought to bring shame.

words.definition: Made to imitate something real in order to cheat people; not genuine.
words.example: The cashier held the bill up to the light and spotted the counterfeit twenty at once.
words.mnemonic: COUNTER-FEIT — made to pass across the shop "counter" as a convincing imitation.

words.definition: Not genuine or true; faked to seem real.
words.example: He got into the club with a bogus ID that listed his age as twenty-five.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "bogey" — a made-up bogeyman isn't real, and neither is this.

words.definition: To invent false information, or to build something from separate parts.
words.example: When questioned, the witness began to fabricate an alibi on the spot.
words.mnemonic: FABRIC — you weave a "fabric" of lies, thread by thread.

words.definition: To copy money, documents, or art so convincingly as to cheat people.
words.example: She was arrested after trying to forge her employer's signature on the checks.
words.mnemonic: A blacksmith's FORGE hammers out metal — the criminal hammers out fake signatures.

words.definition: To make someone believe something untrue through lies or tricks.
words.example: He managed to deceive his parents for months about dropping out of school.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "the sieve" — a liar's promises leak away like water through a sieve.

words.definition: To cause someone to believe something untrue by giving wrong or incomplete information.
words.example: The vague trail signs mislead hikers into thinking the summit is close when hours remain.
words.mnemonic: 'Mis-' (wrong) + 'lead' — to lead someone the wrong way down a path.

words.definition: To trick someone into holding a mistaken belief, often about reality.
words.example: He deluded himself into thinking he would win, ignoring every warning sign.
words.mnemonic: From Latin ludere, 'to play' — a deluded person is being played.

words.definition: To trick a trusting person into accepting a lie or a bad bargain.
words.example: Con artists dupe elderly homeowners into paying for repairs that are never actually made.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'doop' — a 'dope' is easy to dupe, the fool who falls for the scam.

words.definition: To deceive someone through a clever trick or false appearance.
words.example: The salesman hoodwinked her into buying a car with a hidden fault.
words.mnemonic: Pull a 'hood' over someone's eyes and 'wink' — they can't see the trick.

words.definition: To coax someone into doing something using flattery or clever persuasion.
words.example: She inveigled her way into the exclusive party by charming the guard.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-VEIL' — you veil your true motive to lure someone in.

words.definition: To catch someone in a trap or difficult situation they cannot escape.
words.example: The clever contract ensnared him in debt he could never repay.
words.mnemonic: en- + 'snare' — to place someone inside a snare, or trap.

words.definition: Secret agreement between people to cheat or deceive others.
words.example: The two firms were fined for collusion in fixing prices.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'collision' — two parties secretly colliding to cheat.

words.definition: To secretly plot with others, or to pretend not to notice wrongdoing.
words.example: The guards connived with the smugglers, looking away as crates passed.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'con' + 'knives' — con artists sharpening knives in the dark.

words.definition: To secretly plan with others to do something harmful or unlawful.
words.example: The generals conspired to overthrow the president before dawn.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + 'spire' (Latin spirare, breathe) — plotters breathing together in secret.

words.definition: Secret plotting to achieve a goal, or the power to arouse strong curiosity.
words.example: The royal court seethed with intrigue as nobles jockeyed for the king's favor.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'in-TRICK' — a place full of secret tricks and plots.

words.definition: Open and honest in speech, saying exactly what one thinks.
words.example: To be frank, I don't think your plan will work at all.
words.mnemonic: Picture a friend named Frank who always speaks his mind bluntly.

words.definition: Genuine and honest, without pretense or false feeling.
words.example: Her sincere apology moved everyone, because they could tell she truly meant it.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'sine cera' = 'without wax' — pure marble with no wax to hide cracks.

words.definition: The quality of being honest and having firm moral principles.
words.example: A judge of great integrity, she refused every bribe offered to her.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'integer', a whole number — a person who is morally whole and undivided.

words.definition: Consistently telling the truth and reporting facts accurately.
words.example: A veracious witness, she recounted every detail exactly as it had happened.
words.mnemonic: Root 'ver-' means true (as in verify, verdict) — a veracious person deals in the very truth.

words.definition: The habit or practice of not telling the truth.
words.example: The senator's mendacity finally caught up with him when documents exposed years of false claims.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'mendax' (lying) — a story that's been 'mended' is patched together out of lies.

words.definition: A deliberate breaking of faith or trust with someone who relies on you.
words.example: His perfidy stunned them all: the friend they trusted had quietly sold their secrets to rivals.
words.mnemonic: per- (away) + fides (faith) — faith thrown away.

words.definition: Willing to break promises or betray those who place their trust in you.
words.example: The perfidious advisor smiled at the king while plotting nightly with his enemies.
words.mnemonic: per- + fides (faith): with a perfidious ally, the faith just fizzles.

words.definition: The act of betraying someone's confidence, often through deception.
words.example: The general's treachery cost the army the battle when he opened the gates to the enemy.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'treasure-y' — a traitor sells your treasure to the other side.

words.definition: Likely to betray trust, or dangerously deceptive and unstable.
words.example: The treacherous mountain path had already claimed climbers who trusted its loose rocks.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'reach' inside it — you reach onto thin ice that gives way beneath you.

words.definition: Someone who abandons one side or cause to join the opposing one.
words.example: Once a devoted party member, the turncoat now campaigned loudly for his former rivals.
words.mnemonic: Literally turning your coat inside out to reveal the enemy's colors.

words.definition: A person who deserts a group, belief, or set of rules to rebel against it.
words.example: The renegade officer defied his commanders and led a breakaway unit into the hills.
words.mnemonic: Think 're-negate' — someone who negates the oath they once swore.

words.definition: A person who renounces a religion, party, or principle once firmly held.
words.example: Branded an apostate, she was shunned by the faith she had walked away from.
words.mnemonic: Greek apo- (away) + stenai (to stand) — one who stands away from the fold.

words.definition: Tending to avoid giving direct answers or facing something openly.
words.example: Every question about the missing money got an evasive reply that dodged the point.
words.mnemonic: Built on 'evade' — like an escape artist slipping past a straight answer.

words.definition: Difficult to find, catch, or fully understand.
words.example: The elusive fox slipped through every trap the frustrated farmers set for it.
words.mnemonic: 'e-LOOSE-ive' — it stays loose and slides right out of your grip.

words.definition: Taking a long, indirect route rather than a straight path.
words.example: He gave a circuitous explanation that wandered for ten minutes before reaching its point.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'circuit' — going all the way around the circle to get there.

words.definition: To falsely pretend to be someone or something you are not.
words.example: The con artist masqueraded as a wealthy investor to win the family's trust.
words.mnemonic: It hides the word 'masque' (mask) — a masked ball where every identity is concealed.

words.definition: A false reason given to hide the real purpose behind an action.
words.example: He called in sick as a pretext to slip away to the baseball game.
words.mnemonic: 'pre-text' — the text you recite beforehand to cover your true motive.

words.definition: To cheat someone out of money or property through trickery.
words.example: The smooth-talking salesman swindled elderly customers into buying worthless insurance.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dwindle' — your savings dwindle the moment someone swindles you.

words.definition: To illegally take money or property from someone by deception.
words.example: The pair were arrested for defrauding investors of millions through fake accounts.
words.mnemonic: 'de-fraud' — literally to do fraud to a person; the root fraud is right there.

words.definition: To steal money that was entrusted to you, usually by an employer.
words.example: The accountant embezzled company funds into a secret personal account for years.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'em-bezzle' — imagine a sneaky weasel ('bezzle') skimming cash from the till.

words.definition: To rob someone or charge them far too much through trickery.
words.example: Tourists are often fleeced by taxi drivers who wildly inflate the fare.
words.mnemonic: A sheep's fleece is shaved off — to fleece a person is to strip them of money like wool.

words.definition: To cheat or defraud someone, especially by dodging payment owed.
words.example: The contractor bilked his clients, taking their deposits and never returning to work.
words.mnemonic: 'bilk' rhymes with 'milk' — a bilker milks you dry of every last coin.

words.definition: To obtain something through force, threats, or coercive pressure.
words.example: The gang extorted monthly protection money from every shop owner on the block.
words.mnemonic: 'ex-tort' — from Latin 'torquere', to twist; you twist money out of a victim by force.

words.definition: Involving deception intended to gain something unfairly or unlawfully.
words.example: The bank flagged several fraudulent charges on her stolen credit card.
words.mnemonic: It carries the root 'fraud' — a fraudulent deal is one built entirely on fraud.

words.definition: Likely to mislead or give a false impression of the truth.
words.example: The river's calm surface was deceptive, hiding a fierce current just below.
words.mnemonic: From 'deceive' — as a reception receives you, a deception deceives you.

words.definition: Extremely complex and difficult to follow because of many twists and details.
words.example: The tax form's instructions were so convoluted that even the accountant needed an hour to parse them.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + Latin 'volvere' (to roll) — rolled up together like a coiled snake, all twisted and tangled.

words.definition: Meant to instruct, sometimes in a preachy or moralizing way.
words.example: His didactic tone made the dinner feel like a lecture rather than a conversation.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'didaskein' (to teach); sounds like 'did-attic' — picture a stern teacher who lives in the attic, forever giving lessons.

words.definition: Peculiar to one person; a distinctive quirk not shared by others.
words.example: She had the idiosyncratic habit of alphabetizing her spice rack by scent rather than name.
words.mnemonic: idio- (one's own, as in 'idiom') + Greek 'synkrasis' (mixture) — your own personal blend of quirks that nobody else has.

words.definition: Habitually avoiding work or effort; inclined toward laziness.
words.example: Too indolent to cook, he ate cold cereal for dinner three nights running.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + Latin 'dolere' (to feel pain) — someone who won't take any pains, refusing to exert themselves.

words.definition: Showing little energy or spirit; pleasantly slow and relaxed.
words.example: On the languid August afternoon, no one had the will to move from the shaded porch.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'languish' — both from Latin 'languere' (to be weak); a LANGUID day makes you LANGUISH in the heat.

words.definition: A person who thinks or acts independently, refusing to follow the group.
words.example: As the board's lone maverick, she voted against the merger everyone else endorsed.
words.mnemonic: Samuel Maverick, a Texas rancher who refused to brand his cattle — so unbranded strays, and independent nonconformists, became 'mavericks.'

words.definition: Concerned only with making money, at the expense of ethics.
words.example: His mercenary motives showed when he abandoned the charity the moment the grant money dried up.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'merces' (pay, wages) — same root as 'merchant' and 'commerce'; a mercenary works only for the pay.

words.definition: Offering unwanted advice or services in a meddling, bossy manner.
words.example: The officious clerk insisted on rearranging my paperwork twice before he would even look at it.
words.mnemonic: Hides the word 'office' — picture a petty office worker eager to enforce every rule that isn't his to enforce (not the same as 'official').

words.definition: To ease the symptoms of something without removing its cause.
words.example: The medicine could palliate her cough but never cure the underlying illness.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'pallium' (a cloak) — to palliate is to throw a cloak over pain, softening and hiding it rather than removing it.

words.definition: Unwilling to spend money or use resources; excessively frugal.
words.example: So parsimonious was my uncle that he reused tea bags and darned his socks for decades.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'parse-money' — someone who parses every penny, counting cash so carefully they refuse to part with it.

words.definition: Brief and full of meaning; expressing much in few words.
words.example: Her pithy three-word reply said more than his rambling paragraph ever could.
words.mnemonic: The 'pith' is the concentrated core of a plant stem or an orange — something pithy is all core, no filler.

words.definition: A dull, overused remark offered as though it were meaningful.
words.example: At the funeral he could manage only platitudes like 'everything happens for a reason.'
words.mnemonic: Root 'plat-' means flat (as in 'plateau' and 'plate') — a platitude is a flat, stale saying with no life left in it.

words.definition: The quality of being open, honest, and direct in speech.
words.example: With surprising candor, the CEO admitted the product launch had been a failure.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'candor' (whiteness, brightness) — same root as 'candle' and 'candid'; speech so clear it's like bright light, nothing hidden.

words.definition: A thin, attractive surface that hides a rougher or less pleasant reality.
words.example: Beneath his polished veneer of charm lay a cold and calculating negotiator.
words.mnemonic: Literally a thin sheet of fine wood glued over cheap board — a veneer is always a pretty layer covering what's really underneath.

words.definition: A false or misleading outward appearance adopted to hide one's real purpose.
words.example: The con man entered the bank under the guise of a repair technician.
words.mnemonic: It's the root hiding inside DISguise — a guise is the look a disguise gives you.

words.definition: Skilled at getting what one wants through cleverness and trickery.
words.example: The cunning fox faked a limp to lure the hens out of their coop.
words.mnemonic: Say it fast and it sounds like 'conning' — a con artist is cunning.

words.definition: Making a showy pretense of being morally superior to everyone else.
words.example: Her sanctimonious lectures on charity annoyed the volunteers who quietly did the real work.
words.mnemonic: SANCT- means holy (saint, sanctuary) — someone acting holier-than-thou.

words.definition: The practice of claiming beliefs or standards one does not actually follow.
words.example: His anti-smoking speech reeked of hypocrisy, delivered with a lit cigarette in his hand.
words.mnemonic: From Greek for stage-acting — picture a 'hippo-crazy' hippo pretending to be a graceful ballerina.

words.definition: A deceptive front that conceals what something or someone is really like.
words.example: Behind its cheerful facade, the company was quietly drowning in debt.
words.mnemonic: Contains FACE — the polished face a building shows the street while hiding its interior.

words.definition: Sincere and natural, completely free of cunning or deceit.
words.example: The child answered with such artless honesty that she gave away the surprise party.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: ART-LESS — without the 'art' of trickery or guile.

words.definition: A deceptive movement meant to draw an opponent's attention from the real target.
words.example: The boxer threw a feint with his left, then landed a right hook clean on the jaw.
words.mnemonic: Sounds exactly like 'faint' and is cousin to 'feign' — a pretend move, not the real one.

words.definition: To free someone from a mistaken belief or false idea.
words.example: Let me disabuse you of the notion that this promotion will make your job any easier.
words.mnemonic: DIS- (undo) + ABUSE — you undo the mental 'abuse' of a wrong idea someone's been carrying.

words.definition: An unfounded rumor or false story spread to deceive or mislead people.
words.example: The claim that the mayor secretly owns the stadium turned out to be a canard invented by a rival campaign.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "can-nard" — picture a duck (French *canard* = duck) quacking a loud, fake story across the pond.
